findings.where: End of the lesson (explain, practice or a closing SHOW screen)
findings.what: The close the brief promised for this last lesson is missing: nothing says bigger systems are the same row moves run by a computer (the ship's bus admittance matrix and the reactor core code's solver, named as uses), Cramer's rule is never named, the 3 by 3 inverse (an SQA EM4 line) is never named as found by the same row moves or a calculator, and Linear algebra is never named as where hand-worked inverses, rank, pivots and the reduced form go; the only trace is one line in ignores, and lessons 5 and 6 do not cover it either.

The brief's limit on the method, that loop currents work only for circuits that can be drawn flat with no crossing wires, is not stated anywhere; one short sentence after 'Going round each loop gives one equation' would keep the method from reading as universal.

'Double row 2 and add row 1' is the first time a steps screen scales the row being changed, but no screen says that multiplying a row by any number but 0 is safe or why it is done here, which is to turn the −3 into −6 so row 1's 6 clears it in whole numbers; screen 12's puzzle depends on this, so add one short sentence (the text is 49 words, with room).

The rows' numbers are not tied to the drawing; one sentence giving lesson 5's pattern for three loops (down the diagonal is each loop's total resistance, and off it is minus what two loops share) would let him check 6, 12 and −3 against the picture, as the brief promised.

findings.where: Screen 12 (Mixed: clear column 2), feedback and Why?
findings.what: After Check, a 0.5 A arrow appears on the resistor that loops 2 and 3 share, but no sentence says what it is; add to the Why: 'The resistor loops 2 and 3 share carries I₂ − I₃ = −0.5 A. So 0.5 A flows against loop 2's arrow.'

findings.where: Screen 10 (How many answers?) and the lesson's predict
findings.what: The brief asked him to predict from the determinant before the grid is finished, but predict is null and screen 10 hands over the finished staircase; ask 'none, one or a whole line?' from the zero determinant first, then let Check run the moves, so the determinant-only guess is tested.

'Here the bottom row ends up 0 = 5' does not say that a new grid has loaded, so in the read-through, and at first sight, it can seem to be the screen 1 system; lead with 'A new grid, x + y + z = 3, x − y + z = 1 and 2x + 2z = 9.' (43 words now, so there is room).

The sentence 'So all three planes share the line where planes 1 and 2 cross: x = 2 − t, y = 1 and z = t, for any number t.' chains two ideas and brings in t without saying what it is; split it, for example 'All three planes share the line where planes 1 and 2 cross. Each number t picks one point on it: x = 2 − t, y = 1 and z = t.'

Whole grids are written inline as '[1 2 −1 | 4; 2 1 1 | 5; 3 3 0 | 9]', so the task is dense at 360 px (screen 10 has two grids and 46 words) and repeats the grid drawn just below; say 'This staircase' or 'This grid' and let the drawing carry the numbers, keeping inline only the grid the picture does not show.

There are six footnote markers: five sources, plus [^1] again in the bold summary, and [^4] sits on a plain maths fact; cut them to the two or three rules he might look up, the row moves and the loop equations, and drop the repeat from the summary.
Sources 1, 4 and 5 have the title '88', a page number, so their footnotes show a label that means nothing; title them 'HELM Workbook 8: Matrix solution of equations'.
Swapping two rows appears here for the first time, with no reason given that it is safe (the same equations in a different order) and no screen showing it; add that clause.

findings.where: 3-D view, screens 1 and 3 to 5 at 360 px (the opening and moved pictures, light and dark)
findings.what: From the starting angle, plane 1 faces the viewer almost square-on, so the three see-through patches read as flat overlapping shapes until he drags; start the view turned 20 to 30 degrees further so the depth and plane 2's swing about its hinge show without a drag.
